考試官學正呉　批：〔能識出理數之旨，士為佳作。〕

聖人即歸餘蓍數以象月之閏，合乾坤蓍數以象歲之周。蓋蓍策之數與天地之數，無往而不合也；然皆出於理勢之自然，豈人之智力能損益哉？且夫揲蓍
translation_en:
…responds to the Second, it is by means of this Way of centrality and correctness; when the Second responds to the Fifth, it is likewise through this virtue of centrality and correctness. Because both the Second and the Fifth attain centrality and correctness, an enlightened sovereign and a worthy minister meet one another, and ruler and subject are able to encounter the good fortune of flourishing excellence; virtue and beneficence flow forth, and all under heaven are able to receive the blessings of peace and tranquility. Does not the hexagram statement, "It is advantageous to have somewhere to go," take its root right here? I have observed that among the various hexagrams of the Changes, those that speak of "advantage in going" [? 利從, for 利往] do not speak of "advantage in crossing [the great stream]." Why does the Commentary on the Judgments (Tuan) for Increase (Yi) possess both? It is because Increase takes benefiting those below as its root; when the root is firm, there is nothing that is not advantageous. This is why in advancing it is advantageous to go forward, and in crossing over it is advantageous to ford the stream. The Great Commentary (Dazhuan) says: "Increase is for giving rise to benefit." How could one not believe this!

"The remainder is placed between the fingers to symbolize the intercalary month. In five years there are two intercalations, and therefore the remainder is twice placed between the fingers and afterward the next operation is suspended [with a stalk hung between the fingers]. The milfoil stalks of Qian number two hundred and sixteen; the milfoil stalks of Kun number one hundred and forty-four. In all they number three hundred and sixty, corresponding to the days of the cycle of a year."

Associate Examiner Zhou, Assistant Instructor (Xundao), comments: 〔By extending and synthesizing the commentaries and annotations to form the essay, it is far superior to other compositions. "When the thoroughbred〕 〔appears, the herd of horses is left empty"—is this not truly believable?〕

Ao Shan 敖山

Examiner Tang, Instructor (Jiaoyu), comments: 〔On the topic of the method of milfoil divination, where the multitude of candidates fell short, this composition alone grasped it.〕
Examiner Wu, Director of Studies (Xuezheng), comments: 〔Able to discern the import of principle and number; it is [? 士, for 誠] a fine composition.〕

The sages took the numbers of the remaining milfoil stalks placed between the fingers to symbolize the intercalation of months, and combined the numbers of the milfoil stalks of Qian and Kun to symbolize the cycle of a year. Indeed, the numbers of the milfoil stalks and the numbers of Heaven and Earth correspond in every respect; yet all of this arises from the spontaneity of principle and circumstance—how could human intelligence or strength add to or detract from it? Moreover, in the method of sorting the milfoil stalks…

title: 成化元年山東鄉試錄
text:
之法既虛而分既掛而揲各有象矣至歸奇於扐復
何所象哉蓋四數兩手之策必有奇餘之數或一二
焉或三四焉左手者歸于第四第三指之間以象夫
三歲之一閏右手者歸于第三第二指之中以象夫
五歲之再閏五歲之中凡有再閏然後別起積分故
五者之中凡有再扐然後別起一掛聖人即歸餘蓍
數以象月之閏者如此若夫揲蓍三變之末餘三奇
則九其過揲之策亦四九三十有六以此計乾之六
爻則得二百一十有六焉餘三□□□其過揲之策
===
亦四六□□□□□□□坤之六爻則得一百四十
有四焉然總計□□之策有三百六十之數而周歲
之間由春而夏自秋而冬日亦三百六十而是策足
以當之又非聖人合乾坤蓍數以象歲之周乎雖然
蓍數與造化相準不但是也就此章論之由虛一而
歸奇乃天地四時生萬物者也用奇數策數以定陰
陽老少又萬物各正性命於天地者也吁蓍策造化
妙契无間非翼易聖人發明於大傳其孰能知之
書
punctuated:
之法，既虛而分，既掛而揲，各有象矣。至「歸奇於扐」，復何所象哉？蓋四數兩手之策，必有奇餘之數，或一二焉，或三四焉。左手者歸于第四、第三指之間，以象夫三歲之一閏；右手者歸于第三、第二指之中，以象夫五歲之再閏。五歲之中，凡有再閏，然後別起積分；故五者之中，凡有再扐，然後別起一掛。聖人即歸餘蓍數以象月之閏者如此。若夫揲蓍三變之末，餘三奇則九，其過揲之策亦四九三十有六，以此計乾之六爻，則得二百一十有六焉；餘三□□□，其過揲之策亦四六□□□□□□□坤之六爻，則得一百四十有四焉。然總計□□之策，有三百六十之數；而周歲之間，由春而夏，自秋而冬，日亦三百六十，而是策足以當之，又非聖人合乾坤蓍數以象歲之周乎？雖然，蓍數與造化相準，不但是也。就此章論之，由虛一而歸奇，乃天地四時生萬物者也；用奇數、策數以定陰陽老少，又萬物各正性命於天地者也。吁！蓍策造化，妙契无間，非翼《易》聖人發明於《大傳》，其孰能知之！

《書》
translation_en:
…method of sorting yarrow stalks, after setting one aside to represent the void and dividing the rest in two, and after suspending one stalk and counting the remainder by fours, each step has its symbolic counterpart. When it comes to "returning the remainder to the spaces between the fingers," what then does this symbolize? When counting the stalks in both hands by fours, there will inevitably be a remainder—either one or two, or three or four. That from the left hand is placed between the fourth and third fingers to symbolize one intercalary month in three years; that from the right hand is placed between the third and second fingers to symbolize two intercalary months in five years. Within five years there are in all two intercalations, after which the accumulation of fractional days begins anew; therefore, among the five operations there are in all two placements of remainders between the fingers, after which a new suspension of one stalk begins. Such is the way the sages used the yarrow-stalk remainders placed between the fingers to symbolize the intercalary months.

As for the end of the three changes in sorting the yarrow stalks: if the remainders are three odd numbers, the value is nine, and the stalks that have passed through the four-by-four counting are likewise four times nine, or thirty-six; reckoning the six lines of the Qian hexagram on this basis gives two hundred and sixteen. If the remainders are three [even numbers, the value is six], and the stalks that have passed through the counting are likewise four times six, [or twenty-four; reckoning on this basis] the six lines of the Kun hexagram gives one hundred and forty-four. Yet when one totals the stalks of [Qian and Kun], they number three hundred and sixty; and in the cycle of a full year, from spring to summer and from autumn to winter, the days are also three hundred and sixty, so that these stalks suffice to correspond to them. Is this not again the sages' combining the yarrow-stalk numbers of Qian and Kun to symbolize the cycle of the year?

Even so, the correspondence between the yarrow-stalk numbers and the workings of nature does not stop at this alone. Discussing it in terms of this chapter, the progression from setting one stalk aside to returning the remainders between the fingers represents Heaven, Earth, and the four seasons giving birth to the myriad things; and using the numbers of the remainders and the counted stalks to determine old and young yin and yang further represents the myriad things each rectifying its nature and destiny in Heaven and Earth. Alas! The marvelous, seamless accord between the yarrow stalks and the workings of nature—had the sage who wrote the Wings to the Book of Changes (Yi) not elucidated it in the Great Commentary (Dazhuan), who could have known it?

Book of Documents (Shu)

title: 成化元年山東鄉試錄
text:
導沇水東流爲濟入于河溢爲滎東出于陶丘
北又東至荷又東北會于汶又北東入于海
邢端
同考試官訓導羅
批場中作者多爲題所窘是篇深〔合題意盖嘗用心於禹貢者歟〕
考試官教諭柴
批結敘有條且典雅可取
考試官學正吳
批場中作此題詞多鄙澀乃獨順〔可觀當是作者〕
===
聖人於濟水必溯其源之發而順其流之歸也盖濟
水發源於沇而歸宿于海也非聖人濬其源何以得
順流而歸于海哉自今言之治水莫先於隨山亦莫
先於濬川而禹也施濬川之功尤必先於發源之地
焉是故王屋之山泉源所出沇水也濬而滌之則有
以去其壅塞矣然發源爲沇既東爲濟而入于河濟
水勁疾潛行絶河南溢而爲滎盖河濟名也而滎即
滎波之滎乎自滎而出于陶丘北濟水至是常見不
伏又東而至于菏盖陶丘地名也而菏即菏澤之菏
乎濟水至菏豈但止於是哉又東北而會于汶夫濟
punctuated:
「導沇水，東流爲濟，入于河，溢爲滎，東出于陶丘北，又東至于荷，又東北會于汶，又北東入于海。」
邢端
同考試官訓導羅批：場中作者多爲題所窘，是篇深〔合題意，盖嘗用心於《禹貢》者歟。〕
考試官教諭柴批：結敘有條，且典雅可取。
考試官學正吳批：場中作此題，詞多鄙澀，乃獨順〔可觀，當是作者。〕

聖人於濟水，必溯其源之發，而順其流之歸也。盖濟水發源於沇，而歸宿于海也；非聖人濬其源，何以得順流而歸于海哉？自今言之，治水莫先於隨山，亦莫先於濬川；而禹也施濬川之功，尤必先於發源之地焉。是故王屋之山，泉源所出，沇水也；濬而滌之，則有以去其壅塞矣。然發源爲沇，既東爲濟而入于河，濟水勁疾，潛行絶河，南溢而爲滎；盖河、濟名也，而滎即滎波之滎乎！自滎而出于陶丘北，濟水至是常見不伏，又東而至于菏；盖陶丘地名也，而菏即菏澤之菏乎！濟水至菏，豈但止於是哉？又東北而會于汶，夫濟
translation_en:
"He conducted the Yan River, which flowed east to become the Ji, entered the Yellow River, overflowed to form the Xing Marsh, emerged in the east to the north of Taoqiu, went further east to reach the He Marsh, then went northeast to join the Wen River, and then went north and east to enter the sea."

By Xing Duan 邢端.
Associate Examiner Instructor Luo comments: Most candidates in the examination hall were stymied by this topic, yet this essay deeply [accords with the meaning of the topic; surely he is one who has devoted effort to the Tribute of Yu (Yu gong)!]
Examiner Instructor Chai comments: The structure and exposition are orderly, and its classical elegance makes it worthy of selection.
Examiner Director of Studies Wu comments: Among those writing on this topic in the examination hall, the diction was mostly crude and awkward, whereas this alone is smooth [and well worth reading; he is truly a capable writer.]

With regard to the Ji River, the sage necessarily traced where its source springs forth and followed where its current returns. For the Ji River has its source in the Yan and finds its ultimate resting place in the sea; had the sage not dredged its source, how could it have flowed smoothly to return to the sea? Speaking of it today, in regulating the waters nothing takes precedence over following the mountains, nor does anything take precedence over dredging the rivers; and when Yu applied his labor of dredging the rivers, he especially had to begin at the place where the source springs forth. Therefore, the spring that issues from Mount Wangwu is the Yan River; by dredging and clearing it, he was able to remove its blockages. Yet rising at its source as the Yan, once it flows east it becomes the Ji and enters the Yellow River. The waters of the Ji, swift and forceful, travel underground across the Yellow River and overflow to the south to form the Xing; for Yellow River and Ji are river names, and Xing is none other than the Xing of the Xingbo Marsh! From the Xing it emerges to the north of Taoqiu—from this point the waters of the Ji remain constantly visible and do not go underground—and goes further east to reach the He; for Taoqiu is a place name, and He is none other than the He of the Heze Marsh! Having reached the He, how could the Ji River merely stop there? It goes further northeast and joins the Wen River. Now, the Ji…

title: 成化元年山東鄉試錄
text:
汶二水昔也固嘗同流而異派今則勢均相敵會合
而爲一矣濟水會汶豈終于此哉又東北而入于海
夫海所以納百川向也濟固顯伏而不常今則以小
入大朝宗而有歸矣是則濟水若斷若續而同一其
源流必至于海而後已或見或伏而同一其脉絡必
有所止而後已聖人導水之條例史臣得不詳記之
哉抑考禹貢導水九條或先言山而後水或先言水
而後山沇水獨不言山何耶蓋先言山而後水者以
水之源出於山也先言水而後山者以水之源非出
===
於山特自其山以導之耳沇水不言山者沇水伏流
其出非一故不誌其源也此禹貢立言之法也不可
不知
政貴有恒辭尚體要不惟好異商俗靡靡利口
惟賢餘風未殄公其念哉
王綸
同考試官訓導羅　批文詞簡切優於他卷可取
考試官教諭棠　批理明詞順宜用錄出
考試官學正吳　批題不難作者多黏蔡傳先生言
punctuated:
汶二水，昔也固嘗同流而異派，今則勢均相敵，會合而爲一矣。濟水會汶，豈終于此哉？又東北而入于海。夫海所以納百川，向也濟固顯伏而不常，今則以小入大，朝宗而有歸矣。是則濟水若斷若續，而同一其源流，必至于海而後已；或見或伏，而同一其脉絡，必有所止而後已。聖人導水之條例，史臣得不詳記之哉？抑考《禹貢》導水九條，或先言山而後水，或先言水而後山，沇水獨不言山，何耶？蓋先言山而後水者，以水之源出於山也；先言水而後山者，以水之源非出於山，特自其山以導之耳。沇水不言山者，沇水伏流，其出非一，故不誌其源也。此《禹貢》立言之法也，不可不知。

政貴有恒，辭尚體要，不惟好異。商俗靡靡，利口惟賢，餘風未殄，公其念哉！
王綸
同考試官訓導羅　批：文詞簡切，優於他卷，可取。
考試官教諭棠　批：理明詞順，宜用錄出。
考試官學正吳　批：題不難，作者多黏《蔡傳》，先生言
translation_en:
…and Wen rivers in the past had indeed flowed together in different branches, now their forces are evenly matched and they converge to become one. Having joined the Wen, does the Ji River end here? It goes further northeast and enters the sea. Now, the sea is that which receives the hundred rivers. Previously, the Ji had appeared and gone underground irregularly, but now, as the small enters the great, it pays court to the sea and finds its destination. Thus, although the Ji River seems now broken, now continuous, its source and flow are unified, not stopping until it reaches the sea; although it sometimes appears and sometimes flows underground, its veins and channels are unified, not stopping until it reaches its final resting place. Could the historian fail to record in detail the principles by which the sage channeled the waters? Furthermore, if we examine the nine entries on channeling the waters in the "Tribute of Yu" (Yu gong), some mention the mountain first and then the river, while others mention the river first and then the mountain. Why does the entry for the Yan River alone not mention a mountain? Because where the mountain is mentioned first and then the river, it is because the source of the river emerges from that mountain; where the river is mentioned first and then the mountain, it is because the source of the river does not emerge from that mountain, and the river was merely channeled starting from that mountain. As for why no mountain is mentioned for the Yan River, the Yan flows underground and emerges in more than one place, so its source is not recorded. This is the rhetorical method of the "Tribute of Yu," which one must not fail to understand.

"In governance, value constancy; in proclamations, prize substance and essentials. Do not merely delight in novelty. The customs of Shang were sycophantic, deeming sharp tongues alone to be worthy. Remnants of these ways are not yet extinguished; may the Duke bear this in mind!"
Wang Lun 王綸
Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Luo 羅 comments: The wording is concise and to the point, superior to other papers; it may be selected.
Examiner and Instructor Tang 棠 comments: The reasoning is clear and the phrasing smooth; it should be copied out for inclusion.
Examiner and Director of Studies Wu 吳 comments: The topic is not difficult, yet most writers cleave too closely to Cai's Commentary (Cai zhuan). The gentleman's words…

title: 成化元年山東鄉試錄
text:
詞順偉見此篇
賢君於大臣也既欲重治體而守常復欲因習俗而
致慮蓋治體之大在守常而俗之不美所當慮也聖
君於大臣何其戒之切而望之深歟昔康王命畢公
若曰公茲保釐東郊必有政以乂其民也政必貴於
有恒焉政惟有恒則純清而不擾矣公往撫殷遺民
必有辭以播告于下也辭必尚乎體要焉辭惟體要
則典重而不浮矣然政不可以好異也使其異而是
好則悅須臾而厭持久政安能有恒乎辭不可以喜
===
異也使其異而是喜則言有餘而理不足辭安能體
要乎矧商之頑民其俗奢靡而巧言亂昔惟以為賢
昔周簡侈進良矣其餘風猶未息也公可不為之慮
哉洛之遷民其習流蕩而巧言如簧自以為能今雖
世變風移而遺習猶未泯也公可不為之念哉使誠
能以此為念則政無不成而民無不化此康王所以
望畢公之意歟大抵政令之臧否民俗之美惡皆大
臣一身之繫焉且畢公四世元老德業之隆聞望之
尊何政辭之不善民俗之不可化也康王之致告誡
punctuated:
詞，順偉見此篇。
賢君於大臣也，既欲重治體而守常，復欲因習俗而致慮。蓋治體之大在守常，而俗之不美所當慮也。聖君於大臣，何其戒之切而望之深歟！昔康王命畢公若曰：公茲保釐東郊，必有政以乂其民也，政必貴於有恒焉；政惟有恒，則純清而不擾矣。公往撫殷遺民，必有辭以播告于下也，辭必尚乎體要焉；辭惟體要，則典重而不浮矣。然政不可以好異也，使其異而是好，則悅須臾而厭持久，政安能有恒乎？辭不可以喜異也，使其異而是喜，則言有餘而理不足，辭安能體要乎？矧商之頑民，其俗奢靡而巧言亂，昔惟以為賢；昔周簡侈進良矣，其餘風猶未息也，公可不為之慮哉！洛之遷民，其習流蕩而巧言如簧，自以為能；今雖世變風移，而遺習猶未泯也，公可不為之念哉！使誠能以此為念，則政無不成，而民無不化，此康王所以望畢公之意歟！大抵政令之臧否、民俗之美惡，皆大臣一身之繫焉。且畢公四世元老，德業之隆、聞望之尊，何政辭之不善、民俗之不可化也？康王之致告誡…
translation_en:
… wording, whereas smooth and grand expression is seen in this essay.
In dealing with his great ministers, a worthy ruler not only wishes them to value the fundamentals of governance and hold to constancy, but also wishes them to give careful thought in response to popular customs. For the greatness of the fundamentals of governance lies in holding to constancy, while the unwholesomeness of customs is something that must be given careful thought. How earnest are a sage ruler's admonitions to his great minister, and how deep his expectations! In antiquity, King Kang charged the Duke of Bi, saying in effect: "You now go to secure and regulate the eastern outskirts; you must have governance wherewith to bring order to the people, and governance must value constancy. Only when governance has constancy will it be pure and clear without being disruptive. You go to soothe the remnant people of Yin; you must have words wherewith to proclaim instructions to those below, and your words must esteem substance and essentials. Only when words embody substance and essentials will they be dignified and weighty without being superficial. Yet in governance one must not be fond of novelty; if it is novelty that one is fond of, then one will delight in the momentary and grow weary of what endures—how then could governance have constancy? And in words one must not delight in novelty; if it is novelty that one delights in, then words will be in excess while principle falls short—how then could words embody substance and essentials? Moreover, among the recalcitrant people of Shang, their customs are extravagant and decadent, and with artful speech that confounds [or: sharp-tongued speech], in former times they regarded only such men as worthy. Although in the past Zhou has already winnowed out the extravagant and advanced the good, those lingering customs have still not ceased—how could you not give thought to this? Among the relocated people of Luo, their habits are dissipated and unrestrained, and with artful speech like reed-organs they consider themselves capable. Even though times have changed and customs have shifted today, their remnant habits have still not died out—how could you not bear this in mind?" If he could truly bear this in mind, then no governance would fail to succeed and no people would fail to be transformed; was this not the intent of what King Kang hoped for from the Duke of Bi? Broadly speaking, whether government orders are good or bad, and whether popular customs are fine or base, all hinge upon the person of the great minister alone. Furthermore, the Duke of Bi was a senior statesman of four reigns, lofty in virtue and achievement and revered in reputation—how could his governance and words fail to be good, or the people's customs fail to be transformable? That King Kang delivered his admonitions…

title: 成化元年山東鄉試錄
text:
如此厥後道洽政治澤潤生民以收成終之效謂非
得於告戒之力耶
詩
蓺之荏菽荏菽旆旆禾役穟穟麻麥幪幪瓜瓞
唪唪誕后稷之穡有相之道茀厥豐草種之
黃茂
同考試官訓導夏　批〔析理詳明措詞簡當宜居高選〕
考試官教諭桊　批〔平順可取〕
陳鼎
===
考試官學正吳　批〔是作深明后稷之心殊為有得者也〕
聖人之種殖地利者既致生意之盛聖人之相助地
利者必盡農事之宜夫種殖而致地利之盛者固由
於天性之自然也相助以盡農事之宜者豈非其贊
化育之道乎思昔周公制禮尊后稷以配天故推本
而言之若曰后稷當夫岐嶷之時而已好夫種殖之
事其始而種之以荏菽則荏菽之生旆旆然而枝旟
揚起矣繼而樹之以禾稼則禾稼之盛穟穟然而行
列美好矣曰麻曰麥雖彼此之異類莫不幪幪而茂
punctuated:
如此。厥後道洽政治，澤潤生民，以收成終之效，謂非得於告戒之力耶？

《詩》
「蓺之荏菽，荏菽旆旆。禾役穟穟，麻麥幪幪，瓜瓞唪唪。誕后稷之穡，有相之道。茀厥豐草，種之黃茂。」
同考試官訓導夏　批〔析理詳明，措詞簡當，宜居高選。〕
考試官教諭桊　批〔平順可取。〕
陳鼎
考試官學正吳　批〔是作深明后稷之心，殊為有得者也。〕

聖人之種殖地利者，既致生意之盛；聖人之相助地利者，必盡農事之宜。夫種殖而致地利之盛者，固由於天性之自然也；相助以盡農事之宜者，豈非其贊化育之道乎？思昔周公制禮，尊后稷以配天，故推本而言之。若曰：后稷當夫岐嶷之時，而已好夫種殖之事。其始而種之以荏菽，則荏菽之生旆旆然，而枝旟揚起矣；繼而樹之以禾稼，則禾稼之盛穟穟然，而行列美好矣。曰麻曰麥，雖彼此之異類，莫不幪幪而茂
translation_en:
… such as this. Thereafter, when the Way pervaded and governance was well ordered, and blessings moistened the living people so as to reap the effect of bringing the work to a successful completion, could one say that this was not achieved through the power of his admonitions?

Classic of Poetry (Shijing)
"He planted large beans, and the large beans grew with fluttering leaves. His rows of grain were luxuriant in the ear, his hemp and wheat were dense and thick, and his gourds and melons were abundant with fruit. Truly, Hou Ji's husbandry had the way of assisting nature. Having cleared away the thick grass, he sowed the yellow, flourishing grains."
Comment by Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Xia: [The analysis of principles is detailed and clear, and the wording is concise and fitting; he deserves to be placed in a high rank.]
Comment by Examiner and Instructor Quan [?]: [Smooth and acceptable.]
Chen Ding 陳鼎
Comment by Examiner and Subprefectural/Departmental Director of Studies Wu: [This composition deeply understands the mind of Hou Ji; it is truly one that has grasped the meaning.]

When the sage planted and cultivated the bounty of the earth, he already brought about flourishing vitality; when the sage assisted the bounty of the earth, he necessarily exhausted what was proper to agricultural affairs. Now, planting and cultivating so as to bring about the flourishing of the earth's bounty certainly stemmed from the spontaneity of his heavenly nature; and assisting it so as to exhaust what was proper to agricultural affairs—was this not his Way of aiding the transforming and nourishing processes of Heaven and Earth? Thinking back to antiquity, when the Duke of Zhou established the rites and revered Hou Ji as the correlate of Heaven, he traced things back to their origin and spoke of them. It is as if he said: When Hou Ji was at the age of early childhood intelligence, he already loved the business of planting and cultivating. At first, when he planted large beans, the growth of the large beans was fluttering, with branches waving like banners; next, when he set out the grain crops, the flourishing of the grain crops was luxuriant in the ear, with rows fine and regular. As for hemp and wheat, though they are different species from one another, none failed to be dense and thick in their…

title: 成化元年山東鄉試錄
text:
容曰瓜曰瓞雖小大之異名莫不唪唪而多實夫后
稷之種殖如此者非由於習而後能也蓋出於天性
之自然耳夫幼時而好種殖固由其所禀之異及爲
成人而教稼穡又能盡夫人事之宜是以人見其穡
之盛者莫不以爲生物自然之性而不知其能盡人
力之助也人見其穡之美者莫不以爲天地生成之
功而不知其能盡相助之道也然所以相之者盖以
豐草之蕪穢所以妨穀者也則必茀治之而後得以
布其嘉穀焉豐草之□□所以害苗者也則必芟刈
===
之而後可以種之□□□焉夫后稷之穡如此者非忽
易而爲之也盖盡乎人力之助耳抑考思文之詩有
曰粒我烝民莫匪爾極貽我来牟帝命率育凡吾民
得以遂其粒食之願者何莫而非后稷之所賜哉故
帝堯以其有功於民而封於邰也周公制禮尊后稷
以配天而追言及此不亦宜乎
率履不越遂視既發相土烈烈海外有截帝命
不違至于湯齊湯降不遲
朱鼎
punctuated:
容；曰瓜曰瓞，雖小大之異名，莫不唪唪而多實。夫后稷之種殖如此者，非由於習而後能也，蓋出於天性之自然耳。夫幼時而好種殖，固由其所禀之異；及爲成人而教稼穡，又能盡夫人事之宜。是以人見其穡之盛者，莫不以爲生物自然之性，而不知其能盡人力之助也；人見其穡之美者，莫不以爲天地生成之功，而不知其能盡相助之道也。然所以相之者，盖以豐草之蕪穢，所以妨穀者也，則必茀治之，而後得以布其嘉穀焉；豐草之□□，所以害苗者也，則必芟刈之，而後可以種之□□□焉。夫后稷之穡如此者，非忽易而爲之也，盖盡乎人力之助耳。抑考《思文》之詩有曰：「粒我烝民，莫匪爾極。貽我来牟，帝命率育。」凡吾民得以遂其粒食之願者，何莫而非后稷之所賜哉？故帝堯以其有功於民而封於邰也。周公制禮，尊后稷以配天，而追言及此，不亦宜乎？
率履不越，遂視既發。相土烈烈，海外有截。帝命不違，至于湯齊。湯降不遲。
朱鼎
translation_en:
…and dense; as for the melons and the young gourds, though differing in name according to whether they were large or small, none failed to be prolific and abundant in fruit. Now, that Houji's planting and cultivation were like this was not something he became capable of only after practice; rather, it sprang from the spontaneity of his heavenly nature. In childhood he was fond of planting and cultivating, which indeed came from his extraordinary natural endowment; and when he reached adulthood and taught sowing and reaping, he was furthermore able to exhaust all that was proper in human effort. Therefore, when people saw the abundance of his husbandry, none failed to take it as the spontaneous nature of living things, not knowing that he was able to exhaust the assistance of human effort; when people saw the excellence of his husbandry, none failed to take it as the generative achievement of Heaven and Earth, not knowing that he was able to exhaust the Way of assisting nature. Yet the means by which he assisted it was that, because the rank overgrowth of lush weeds was what hindered the grain, he 반드시 cleared and dress-tilled them away before he could spread his fine grain there; and because the [?] of lush weeds was what harmed the sprouts, he necessarily mowed and cut them down before he could plant the [?] (yellow-grained millet) there. Now, that Houji's husbandry was like this was not something done negligently or lightly; rather, it exhausted the assistance of human effort. Moreover, if we examine the ode "Siwen" (Accomplished), it says: "You gave grain to our multitudinous people; there is nothing that is not the result of your perfection. You bequeathed to us the wheat and barley, which God on High commanded for universal nourishment." For all our people to be able to fulfill their wish for grain to eat—how could any of it not be the gift of Houji? Therefore Emperor Yao, because of his merit toward the people, enfeoffed him at Tai. When the Duke of Zhou instituted the rites, honoring Houji as the correlate of Heaven, and traced his account back to this—was it not indeed fitting?

"He followed the path without transgressing; then, looking upon them, he saw their response already aroused. Xiangtu was glorious and ardent, and beyond the seas all was brought into orderly submission. The mandate of God on High did not depart, down to Tang, with whom it came into full accord. Tang's birth was not too late."
By Zhu Ding 朱鼎.

title: 成化元年山東鄉試錄
text:
同考試官訓導吳　批〔此場中作者泛泛不切惟此篇詞簡理明宜取以為本房之冠〕
考試官教諭柴　批〔旨明詞順宜在高選〕
考試官學正吳　批〔詞簡而意足可薦何恭〕
君德感人而後王之興廣其業上天眷德而聖人之
生應其時夫德者得天感人之本也今前王之德既
足以感人得天而廣其業矣則聖人之應期而生者
又豈偶然者哉且夫玄王之生也既異於人而其德
也必由乎禮是故動而皆理也有典有則不違乎矩
===
範焉行而皆法也可儀可式不越乎禮度焉是以遂
視其民而民之得於觀感者莫不起而應之以上臨
下而人之獲夫瞻仰者靡不順而從之矣玄王往矣
相土繼之其王業至此時也益烈烈然而光大其國
勢於斯時也愈赫赫然而明顯於是諸侯雖衆無不
帖然而來歸海外雖遠罔不截然而整齊矣夫人心
之所在即天命之所歸是故時雖有先後而皇矣上
帝所以眷顧於有商者不以先後而或殊世雖有遠
近而彼蒼者天所以默契於商家者不以久遠而或
punctuated:
同考試官訓導吳　批〔此場中作者泛泛不切，惟此篇詞簡理明，宜取以為本房之冠。〕
考試官教諭柴　批〔旨明詞順，宜在高選。〕
考試官學正吳　批〔詞簡而意足，可薦何恭。〕

君德感人，而後王之興廣其業；上天眷德，而聖人之生應其時。夫德者，得天感人之本也。今前王之德，既足以感人得天而廣其業矣，則聖人之應期而生者，又豈偶然者哉？且夫玄王之生也，既異於人，而其德也，必由乎禮。是故動而皆理也，有典有則，不違乎矩範焉；行而皆法也，可儀可式，不越乎禮度焉。是以遂視其民，而民之得於觀感者，莫不起而應之；以上臨下，而人之獲夫瞻仰者，靡不順而從之矣。玄王往矣，相土繼之，其王業至此時也，益烈烈然而光大；其國勢於斯時也，愈赫赫然而明顯。於是諸侯雖衆，無不帖然而來歸；海外雖遠，罔不截然而整齊矣。夫人心之所在，即天命之所歸。是故時雖有先後，而皇矣上帝所以眷顧於有商者，不以先後而或殊；世雖有遠近，而彼蒼者天所以默契於商家者，不以久遠而或
translation_en:
Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Wu's comment: [Among the candidates in this session, the writers are generally superficial and miss the mark; only this essay has concise phrasing and clear principles, and ought to be selected as the top paper of this examination ward.]
Examiner and Instructor Chai's comment: [The purport is clear and the diction smooth; it deserves a high ranking.]
Examiner and Director of Studies Wu's comment: [The phrasing is concise yet the meaning is full; it can be recommended, He Gong [?].]

A ruler's virtue moves people, and with the rise of a succeeding king, he expands his enterprise; High Heaven favors virtue, and the birth of a sage corresponds to the proper time. Now, virtue is the foundation for winning Heaven and moving people. Since the virtue of the former kings was already sufficient to move people, win Heaven, and expand their enterprise, how then could the birth of a sage in response to the appointed age be a mere coincidence?

Moreover, as for the birth of the Dark King (Xuanwang 玄王, i.e., Xie 契), he was already extraordinary among men, and in his virtue, he invariably abided by propriety. Therefore, his every movement was in accord with principle—possessing canons and standards, never departing from the proper measure; his every action was a model—worthy of imitation and emulation, never transgressing the bounds of ritual. Thus, when he consequently looked upon his people, among those who were inspired by observing him, there were none who did not rise up in response; when he presided over those below from above, among those who were able to look up to him in reverence, there were none who did not順ly submit and follow him.

When the Dark King passed on, Xiangtu 相土 succeeded him. By this time, the royal enterprise grew ever more blazingly glorious and grand; at this juncture, the power of the state became ever more brilliantly manifest. Thereupon, numerous as the feudal lords were, none failed to come in docile submission; distant as the lands beyond the seas were, none failed to be brought into uniform order.

Now, where the hearts of the people reside is precisely where the Mandate of Heaven turns. Therefore, although times may be earlier or later, the favor with which August Sovereign on High regarded the house of Shang did not vary on account of being earlier or later; although generations may be distant or near, the tacit accord that the Azure Heaven above maintained with the house of Shang was not [interrupted] on account of the passage of time…

title: 成化元年山東鄉試錄
text:
間是以天命方集於商也適湯之生天命至此而大
集王業方歸於商也適湯之出王業於此而有成故
湯之生也不先時而早焉不後時而遲焉天人符合
之妙不期其同而自同彼此感遇之機不期其會而
自會故曰湯降不遲良有以夫抑考是詩序以為大
禘之詩或又以為祫祭之詩首章言濬哲維商長發
其祥所以見湯之有賢君也次章言玄王桓撥又所
以見湯之有武德也至此又言相土之興有以大其
王業下章又言成湯之生有以合乎天命下章又載
===
言湯之載旆末章言伊尹之阿衡左右一詩之
中反覆詠嘆之不足登歌之際洋洋盈耳為商之後
王者寧不有感于中乎
春秋
春王正月〔隱公元年〕滕子來朝〔桓公二年〕荊人來聘〔莊公二十三年〕公會晉侯齊侯宋公蔡侯鄭伯衛子莒子
盟于踐土　公朝于王所〔僖公二十八年〕天王使宰
周公來聘〔僖公三十年〕
punctuated:
間。是以天命方集於商也，適湯之生，天命至此而大集；王業方歸於商也，適湯之出，王業於此而有成。故湯之生也，不先時而早焉，不後時而遲焉。天人符合之妙，不期其同而自同；彼此感遇之機，不期其會而自會。故曰「湯降不遲」，良有以夫！抑考是詩，序以為大禘之詩，或又以為祫祭之詩。首章言「濬哲維商，長發其祥」，所以見湯之有賢君也；次章言「玄王桓撥」，又所以見湯之有武德也；至此又言相土之興，有以大其王業；下章又言成湯之生，有以合乎天命；下章又載言湯之載旆；末章言伊尹之阿衡左右。一詩之中，反覆詠嘆之不足，登歌之際，洋洋盈耳，為商之後王者，寧不有感于中乎？

春秋
「春王正月」〔隱公元年〕，「滕子來朝」〔桓公二年〕，「荊人來聘」〔莊公二十三年〕，「公會晉侯、齊侯、宋公、蔡侯、鄭伯、衛子、莒子盟于踐土，公朝于王所」〔僖公二十八年〕，「天王使宰周公來聘」〔僖公三十年〕。
translation_en:
…interrupted. Therefore, just as the Mandate of Heaven was concentrating upon Shang, it coincided with the birth of Tang, and with this the Mandate of Heaven was grandly concentrated; just as the kingly enterprise was turning toward Shang, it coincided with the emergence of Tang, and herewith the kingly enterprise was brought to completion. Thus, in being born, Tang was neither ahead of the time and too early, nor behind the time and too late. In the wondrous correspondence of Heaven and man, without expecting to coincide, they coincided of themselves; in the pivotal moment of mutual resonance and encounter, without expecting to meet, they met of themselves. Thus when it says, "Tang's descent was not late," there is truly good reason for it!

Moreover, if we examine this ode, the Preface takes it to be an ode for the great Imperial Sacrifice (di), while others take it to be an ode for the Collective Ancestral Sacrifice (xia). The first stanza says, "Profound and wise was Shang, long had its auspicious signs been manifested," so as to show that before Tang there were worthy rulers. The second stanza says, "The Dark King vigorously governed," further showing that before Tang there was martial virtue. Coming to this stanza, it speaks further of the rise of Xiangtu as having enlarged its kingly enterprise. The next stanza speaks further of the birth of Cheng Tang as having accorded with the Mandate of Heaven; the stanza after that again records Tang's raising of his banners; and the final stanza speaks of Yi Yin's assisting on the left and right as Supporting Minister (Aheng). Within a single ode, it chants and sighs over these things repeatedly without end; when sung upon ascent in the hall, the music fills the ears in vast abundance. How could those who came after as kings of Shang not be moved within their hearts?

Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)

"In spring, the king's first month" [first year of Duke Yin]; "The Viscount of Teng came to court" [second year of Duke Huan]; "A man of Jing came on a mission of friendly inquiry" [twenty-third year of Duke Zhuang]; "The Duke met the Marquis of Jin, the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Cai, the Earl of Zheng, the Viscount of Wei, and the Viscount of Ju, and covenanted at Jiantu; the Duke had audience at the King's residence" [twenty-eighth year of Duke Xi]; "The Heavenly King sent the Grand宰 (Zai), the Duke of Zhou, to come on a mission of friendly inquiry" [thirtieth year of Duke Xi].

title: 成化元年山東鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭徐　批〔此篇能以點陟朝聘立說是有見〕〔習是之高選允合輿情〕
考試官教諭柴　批〔義理純正詞氣森嚴不常瓊〕〔杯玉筆爛然可珍〕
考試官學正吳　批〔議論英發文氣老成場中似〕〔此其可多得也耶〕
王道明而黜陟之典行於內外王室尊而朝聘之禮
通乎上下此聖人作經之用晉文尊周之效皆春秋
之義事也恩昔周綱陵夷侯度蔡壞王道不明久矣
===
尚望其行黜陟之典哉故夫子作經首書春王正月
者明王道也以王次春示人君當法天時而賞罰非
天不行也以正次王戒諸侯當遵王朔而政教非王
不舉也大一統之義著君天下之體存王道於是明
矣惟其明王道故滕以侯爵之邦首因朝桓而稱子
黜之也黜之何如桓以不義得國滕之朝桓黨惡矣
則必奉天討以行罰焉荊本蠻夷之國繼因聘魯而
書人陟之也陟之何如魯乃文獻之邦荊之聘為慕
義矣則必奉天命以行賞焉黜陟之典行於內外如
punctuated:
同考試官教諭徐　批：〔此篇能以點陟、朝聘立說，是有見〕〔習是之高選，允合輿情。〕
考試官教諭柴　批：〔義理純正，詞氣森嚴，不常瓊〕〔杯玉筆，爛然可珍。〕
考試官學正吳　批：〔議論英發，文氣老成，場中似〕〔此，其可多得也耶？〕

王道明而黜陟之典行於內外，王室尊而朝聘之禮通乎上下。此聖人作經之用、晉文尊周之效，皆《春秋》之義事也。恩昔周綱陵夷，侯度蔡壞，王道不明久矣，尚望其行黜陟之典哉？故夫子作經，首書「春王正月」者，明王道也。以「王」次「春」，示人君當法天時，而賞罰非天不行也；以「正」次「王」，戒諸侯當遵王朔，而政教非王不舉也。大一統之義著，君天下之體存，王道於是明矣。惟其明王道，故滕以侯爵之邦，首因朝桓而稱「子」，黜之也。黜之何如？桓以不義得國，滕之朝桓，黨惡矣，則必奉天討以行罰焉。荊本蠻夷之國，繼因聘魯而書「人」，陟之也。陟之何如？魯乃文獻之邦，荊之聘為慕義矣，則必奉天命以行賞焉。黜陟之典行於內外如…
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Xu, Instructor, comments: [This essay is able to establish its argument on the basis of demotion and promotion, and of court visits and missions of friendly inquiry; it shows insight into the top selections of those who study this [?], truly according with public sentiment.]
Examiner Chai, Instructor, comments: [The principles and reasoning are pure and upright, and the diction and tone are stern and rigorous; not merely [?] a jade cup or jade brush, it is brilliant and worthy of being treasured.]
Examiner Wu, Director of Studies, comments: [The argumentation is spirited and brilliant, and the literary vitality is mature and accomplished; in the examination compound, how could essays like this be found in great numbers?]

When the Kingly Way is made manifest, the canons of demotion and promotion are carried out both within and without; when the Royal House is honored, the rites of court visits and missions of friendly inquiry circulate between superior and inferior. Such are the function of the Sage in composing the Classic and the efficacy of Duke Wen of Jin in honoring Zhou—both being righteous matters of the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu). Thinking back [?] to the past, when the royal纲 (guiding threads) of Zhou declined and the behavioral standards of the feudal lords collapsed [?], the Kingly Way had long been obscured—how could one still hope for the canons of demotion and promotion to be carried out? Therefore, when the Master composed the Classic, his first writing of "Spring, the King's First Month" was to make manifest the Kingly Way. By placing "King" after "Spring," he indicated that the ruler of men ought to model himself on the seasons of Heaven, and that rewards and punishments are not carried out unless on behalf of Heaven; by placing "First [Month]" after "King," he admonished the feudal lords that they ought to observe the royal calendar, and that governance and instruction are not instituted unless by the King. The principle of Grand Unity was thereby made clear, the constitutional order of ruling all under Heaven was preserved, and thus the Kingly Way was made manifest. Precisely because it made manifest the Kingly Way, Teng, though a state of marquis rank, was first referred to as "Viscount" on account of paying a court visit to Duke Huan—this was to demote him. Why demote him? Huan had obtained his state through unrighteousness, so Teng's paying a court visit to Huan was to side with evil; thus it was necessary to carry out punishment in accordance with Heaven's chastisement. Jing [Chu] was originally a state of the southern barbarians, yet subsequently, on account of sending a mission of friendly inquiry to Lu, its envoy was recorded as "a man [person]"—this was to promote it. Why promote it? Lu was a state of cultural heritage and worthy traditions, so Jing's mission of friendly inquiry was an act of admiring righteousness; thus it was necessary to bestow reward in accordance with Heaven's mandate. That the canons of demotion and promotion were carried out both within and without like…

title: 成化元年山東鄉試錄
text:
此豈不由王道明乎若夫齊桓既往中國無伯王室不
尊甚矣況望其行朝聘之禮哉故晉文主盟而有踐
土之役者尊王室也獻俘衛雍非諂也所以致敵愾
之功要言王庭非慢也所以伸同獎之約尊卑之分
明上下之禮定王室於是尊矣惟其尊王室故魯僖
以秉禮之君率列辟爲王所之朝是朝之感於義也
不然踐土以前玉帛之覲何一不見于周與宰閱以
三公之貴銜王命爲聘魯之舉是聘之激於伯也否
則王所之先周之□□□一不遣于僖與朝聘之禮
===
通乎上下如此豈不由王室尊乎雖然以事功論之
則文或可與夫子比舉道德論之文豈終夫子匹哉
觀其明王道而卒有以感天道故西狩之麟自至尊
王室而終有以慢王室故翟泉之分遂犯此王伯所
以異者在此與
宋公齊侯遇于梁丘〔莊公三十二年〕齊侯宋公江人黃
人盟于貫〔僖公二年〕齊侯宋公江人黃人會于陽
穀〔僖公三年〕遂伐楚　楚屈完來盟于師盟于召
陵　齊人執陳轅濤塗　及江人黃人伐陳
punctuated:
此，豈不由王道明乎？若夫齊桓既往，中國無伯，王室不尊甚矣，況望其行朝聘之禮哉？故晉文主盟而有踐土之役者，尊王室也。獻俘衛雍，非諂也，所以致敵愾之功；要言王庭，非慢也，所以伸同獎之約。尊卑之分明，上下之禮定，王室於是尊矣。惟其尊王室，故魯僖以秉禮之君，率列辟爲王所之朝，是朝之感於義也。不然，踐土以前，玉帛之覲何一不見于周與？宰閱以三公之貴，銜王命爲聘魯之舉，是聘之激於伯也。否則，王所之先，周之□□□一不遣于僖與？朝聘之禮通乎上下如此，豈不由王室尊乎？雖然，以事功論之，則文或可與夫子比；舉道德論之，文豈終夫子匹哉？觀其明王道而卒有以感天道，故西狩之麟自至；尊王室而終有以慢王室，故翟泉之分遂犯。此王伯所以異者在此與！
宋公、齊侯遇于梁丘〔莊公三十二年〕。齊侯、宋公、江人、黃人盟于貫〔僖公二年〕。齊侯、宋公、江人、黃人會于陽穀〔僖公三年〕。遂伐楚。楚屈完來盟于師，盟于召陵。齊人執陳轅濤塗。及江人、黃人伐陳。
translation_en:
…this—how could it not be because the Kingly Way was made manifest? As for the time after Duke Huan of Qi (Qi Huan) had passed away, the Central States lacked a Hegemon, and the Royal House was gravely lacking in veneration—how much less could one hope for the rites of court audience and missions of friendly inquiry to be practiced? Therefore, that Duke Wen of Jin (Jin Wen) presided over the covenants and undertook the campaign of Jiantu was to honor the Royal House. Presenting captives at Weiyong was not flattery; it was the means to deliver the achievement of venting righteous anger against the king's enemies. Exacting a solemn oath in the royal court was not disrespect; it was the means to extend the covenant of jointly supporting the royal house. The distinction between noble and lowly was made clear, the rites between superior and inferior were settled, and thereupon the Royal House was honored. Precisely because he honored the Royal House, Duke Xi of Lu (Lu Xi), as a ruler who upheld ritual, led the various lords to pay court audience at the King's Residence—this was a court audience inspired by righteousness. Otherwise, prior to Jiantu, why was not a single audience offering jade and silk seen in Zhou? Prime Minister Yue (Zai Yue), with the noble rank of one of the Three Dukes, bore the royal command to undertake a mission of friendly inquiry to Lu—this was a mission stimulated by the Hegemon. Otherwise, prior to the audience at the King's Residence, [why was?] Zhou's […] not once dispatched to Duke Xi? That the rites of court audience and missions of friendly inquiry communicated between superior and inferior in this manner—how could it not be because the Royal House was honored? Even so, if one discusses it in terms of deeds and achievements, then Duke Wen might perhaps be compared with the Master [Confucius]; if one raises the discussion to moral virtue, how could Duke Wen ultimately be the Master's peer? Observe how the Master made manifest the Kingly Way and ultimately had that by which he moved the Way of Heaven, so that the unicorn of the western hunt arrived of its own accord; whereas Duke Wen honored the Royal House and yet in the end did that by which he slighted the Royal House, so that the hierarchical distinctions at Diquan were consequently violated. That wherein the Kingly Way and the Way of the Hegemon differ lies right here, does it not?

The Duke of Song and the Marquis of Qi met at Liangqiu [32nd year of Duke Zhuang]. The Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the men of Jiang, and the men of Huang covenanted at Guan [2nd year of Duke Xi]. The Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the men of Jiang, and the men of Huang met at Yanggu [3rd year of Duke Xi]. Thereupon they invaded Chu. Qu Wan of Chu came to covenant with the army, and they covenanted at Shaoling. The men of Qi seized Yuan Taotu of Chen. Together with the men of Jiang and the men of Huang, [Lu] invaded Chen…

title: 成化元年山東鄉試錄
text:
公孫茲帥師會齊人宋人衛人鄭人許人曹
人侵陳〔僖公四年〕公及齊侯宋公陳侯衛侯鄭伯
許男曹伯會王世子于首止　諸侯盟于首
止　鄭伯逃歸不盟　楚人滅弦〔僖公五年〕楚人
圍許〔僖公六年〕
同考試官教諭徐　　　　馬惇
批〔場中作是題者率皆分截字句獨此〕〔深得其旨宜冠本房〕
考試官教諭□
批〔伯主謙驕人心向背之機也作者善於〕
===
〔形容允爲佳士〕
考試官學正吳
批〔發明聖筆力挫楚驕經中之錦也〕
伯德謙而人心從遂致外夷之服伯志驕而人心違
復啓外夷之横此齊桓謙以得諸侯而制楚驕以失
諸侯而縱楚也春秋備書以示勸戒何其至歟且齊
桓之圖楚也非一日矣使桓驕以處已則人心不服
其事有能集乎故梁丘之遇資宋以謀鄭序爵以尊
宋不敢以勢而驕人惟欲先彼而後已桓德一謙人
心大順始焉盟貫澤而宋公江黄自來繼焉會陽穀
punctuated:
公孫茲帥師，會齊人、宋人、衛人、鄭人、許人、曹人侵陳。〔僖公四年〕公及齊侯、宋公、陳侯、衛侯、鄭伯、許男、曹伯會王世子于首止。諸侯盟于首止。鄭伯逃歸不盟。楚人滅弦。〔僖公五年〕楚人圍許。〔僖公六年〕
同考試官教諭徐、馬惇批：〔場中作是題者，率皆分截字句，獨此〕〔深得其旨，宜冠本房。〕
考試官教諭□批：〔伯主謙驕，人心向背之機也。作者善於〕〔形容，允爲佳士。〕
考試官學正吳批：〔發明聖筆，力挫楚驕，經中之錦也。〕
伯德謙而人心從，遂致外夷之服；伯志驕而人心違，復啓外夷之横。此齊桓謙以得諸侯而制楚，驕以失諸侯而縱楚也。《春秋》備書以示勸戒，何其至歟！且齊桓之圖楚也，非一日矣。使桓驕以處已，則人心不服，其事有能集乎？故梁丘之遇，資宋以謀鄭，序爵以尊宋，不敢以勢而驕人，惟欲先彼而後已。桓德一謙，人心大順。始焉盟貫澤，而宋公、江、黄自來；繼焉會陽穀，
translation_en:
… Gongsun Zi led a force to join the men of Qi, the men of Song, the men of Wei, the men of Zheng, the men of Xu, and the men of Cao in making an incursion into Chen. [Fourth year of Duke Xi.] The Duke, along with the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Baron of Xu, and the Earl of Cao, met the royal heir apparent at Shouzhi. The feudal lords made a covenant at Shouzhi. The Earl of Zheng fled home without joining the covenant. The men of Chu extinguished Xian. [Fifth year of Duke Xi.] The men of Chu besieged Xu. [Sixth year of Duke Xi.]

Associate Examiner and County Director of Studies Xu, [writing on the essay of] Ma Dun, comments: [In the examination hall, those who wrote on this topic generally chopped it up into isolated words and phrases; this essay alone] [deeply grasps its meaning and deserves to top this examination ward.]

Examiner and County Director of Studies [?] comments: [The humility or arrogance of a hegemon is the pivot upon which people's allegiance or defection turns. The author excels at] [depicting this, and is truly a fine scholar.]

Examiner and Subprefectural Director of Studies Wu comments: [He elucidates the Sage's brush and forcefully checks the arrogance of Chu; it is a brocade among the essays on the Classics.]

When the hegemon's virtue was humble, people's hearts followed him, thereby bringing about the submission of the outer barbarians; when the hegemon's will grew arrogant, people's hearts turned against him, once again opening the way for the rampant behavior of the outer barbarians. Thus Duke Huan of Qi, through humility, won over the feudal lords and kept Chu in check, and through arrogance, lost the feudal lords and let Chu run rampant. How thorough are the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) in recording all of this to display encouragement and warning!

Moreover, Duke Huan of Qi's planning against Chu was not the work of a single day. Had Huan conducted himself with arrogance, people's hearts would not have submitted; how then could his enterprise have been accomplished? Therefore, at the meeting at Liangqiu, he relied on Song to plan against Zheng, and ordered the ranks of nobility so as to honor Song; he did not dare use his power to treat others arrogantly, desiring only to put others first and himself last. Once Huan's virtue showed humility, people's hearts came into great accord. First, when he made a covenant at Guanze, the Duke of Song and the states of Jiang and Huang came of their own accord; next, when he held an assembly at Yanggu, …

title: 成化元年山東鄉試錄
text:
而宋公江黃復至內舉上公之宋則諸侯無有不服
外言遠國江黃則小大無有不孚人心從矣伯討舉
焉由是征貢之師方抵于江漢而請盟之使遂致乎
屈完退舍召陵而盟禮定強楚貼服而中國安書曰
謙受益桓於此得之矣謙德之效至是盛矣使公善
於持久則人心自固其事有不終乎何乃怒陳誤軍
既執濤塗而復伐以江黃之師未及旋踵而又侵以大
夫之衆楚□無□□道□之貫陳反被拘執侵陵之
患桓志一驕人□□自止之會尊世子也而蔡卒
===
不與同好之盟鄭□□□而鄭復見逃蔡不與則諸
侯無宗伯之心鄭見逃則列國有去齊之志人心違
矣楚復横焉故□□之舉敢為中國之抗圍許之役
以兆北圖之機諸侯自救之不暇而桓伯為之浸衰
矣書曰滿招損桓於此失之矣大抵人道惡盈而好謙
理之常也桓一謙盈而人心所應如此信不誣矣亦
豈不由管仲諫否於其間哉始也桓之謙仲必能諫
故君臣俱有謙享之道終也桓之驕仲不能諫故君
臣俱墮驕盈之域立心既殊得效亦異此夫子所以
punctuated: 而宋公、江、黃復至。內舉上公之宋，則諸侯無有不服；外言遠國江、黃，則小大無有不孚。人心從矣，伯討舉焉。由是征貢之師方抵于江、漢，而請盟之使遂致乎屈完。退舍召陵而盟禮定，強楚貼服而中國安。《書》曰：「謙受益。」桓於此得之矣。謙德之效，至是盛矣。使公善於持久，則人心自固，其事有不終乎？何乃怒陳誤軍，既執濤塗，而復伐以江、黃之師；未及旋踵，而又侵以大夫之衆？楚□無□□道□之貫，陳反被拘執侵陵之患。桓志一驕，人□□自。首止之會，尊世子也，而蔡卒不與；同好之盟，鄭□□□，而鄭復見逃。蔡不與，則諸侯無宗伯之心；鄭見逃，則列國有去齊之志。人心違矣，楚復横焉。故□□之舉，敢為中國之抗；圍許之役，以兆北圖之機。諸侯自救之不暇，而桓伯為之浸衰矣。《書》曰：「滿招損。」桓於此失之矣。大抵人道惡盈而好謙，理之常也。桓一謙盈而人心所應如此，信不誣矣。亦豈不由管仲諫否於其間哉？始也桓之謙，仲必能諫，故君臣俱有謙享之道；終也桓之驕，仲不能諫，故君臣俱墮驕盈之域。立心既殊，得效亦異。此夫子所以
translation_en:
…and the Duke of Song, along with Jiang and Huang, arrived once more. Within the central states, by citing Song, which held the rank of Highest Duke, none among the feudal lords failed to submit; outside, by speaking of the distant states of Jiang and Huang, none, great or small, failed to trust him. Once people's hearts followed him, the hegemon's punitive expedition was launched. Thus, no sooner had the army demanding tribute reached the Jiang and Han rivers than the envoy requesting a covenant arrived in the person of Qu Wan. Retreating a stage to Shaoling, the rites of the covenant were settled; powerful Chu was brought into submissive compliance, and the Central States were at peace. The Book of Documents says: "Humility receives benefit." Huan achieved this here! The efficacy of the virtue of humility reached its height at this point.

Had the Duke been good at persevering, people's hearts would naturally have remained firm—how could his enterprise have failed to reach completion? Why then did he grow angry at Chen for misdirecting the army, first seizing Yuan Taotu and then attacking Chen with the troops of Jiang and Huang, and before he had even turned on his heel, invading it again with a host led by great officers? Chu [?] suffered no [?] punishment for its crimes [?], whereas Chen instead suffered the calamity of seizure and invasion. Once Huan's ambition grew arrogant, people's hearts [?] departed [?]. At the meeting of Shouzhi, which was to honor the Heir Apparent, Cai ultimately did not participate; at the covenant of shared amity, Zheng [?], and Zheng again was recorded as having fled. That Cai did not participate meant the feudal lords lacked the heart to honor the hegemon; that Zheng was recorded as having fled meant the various states harbored the intention of abandoning Qi. Once people's hearts turned away, Chu again grew rampant. Therefore, in the action of [?], it dared to stand in defiance of the Central States, and the campaign of besieging Xu presaged its design to plot against the north. The feudal lords had no leisure even to save themselves, and Huan's hegemony gradually declined because of it. The Book of Documents says: "Fullness invites loss." Huan lost it here!

In general, the way of humanity hates fullness and loves humility; this is the constant principle. Between Huan's humility and his fullness, the response of people's hearts was thus—truly this is no falsehood! And how could this not also be due to whether Guan Zhong remonstrated with him in the interim? In the beginning, when Huan was humble, Zhong must have been able to remonstrate, and thus ruler and minister both possessed the way of humility and success; in the end, when Huan grew arrogant, Zhong was unable to remonstrate, and thus ruler and minister both fell into the realm of arrogance and fullness. Since the intentions they established were different, the effects they obtained also differed. This is why the Master…

title: 成化元年山東鄉試錄
text:
天齊桓之功而小管仲之器者有以夫
禮記
制三公一命卷若有加則賜也不過九命
楊溥
考試官教諭梁
批禮經義貴典而有則此作得之
考試官學正吳
批場中作此題者多龐雜不類此篇
能以詞達理誠禮經之優者
諸大臣命服之□雖出於恩錫然限不可有踰蓋
三公有命服之常□然而特恩有加亦止於九命
===
夫豈可又有所踰□□記王制者謂夫先王建官而有
三公太師太傅太保是也論道經邦任亦大矣燮理
陰陽職亦重焉命以授爵而其制曆八命之榮服以
顯庸而其制用鷩冕之章矣其有一命之加則至於
九命之等處上公之位而服有降龍之袞冕同王者
之後而被無升龍之袞服若為三公而有袞冕之加
者是出於特恩之賜豈八命當然之例乎如為三公
而有袞服之增者乃由於異寵之錫豈鷩冕當用之
制乎然人臣命數止於其九自五命至於七命固有
punctuated:
天齊桓之功而小管仲之器者，有以夫！

《禮記》
「制：三公一命卷，若有加，則賜也，不過九命。」
楊溥
考試官教諭梁批：禮經義貴典而有則，此作得之。
考試官學正吳批：場中作此題者多龐雜不類，此篇能以詞達理，誠《禮記》之優者。

諸大臣命服之□，雖出於恩錫，然限不可有踰。蓋三公有命服之常□，然而特恩有加，亦止於九命，夫豈可又有所踰□□？記《王制》者謂：夫先王建官而有三公，太師、太傅、太保是也。論道經邦，任亦大矣；燮理陰陽，職亦重焉。命以授爵，而其制膺八命之榮；服以顯庸，而其制用鷩冕之章矣。其有一命之加，則至於九命之等；處上公之位，而服有降龍之袞冕；同王者之後，而被無升龍之袞服。若為三公而有袞冕之加者，是出於特恩之賜，豈八命當然之例乎？如為三公而有袞服之增者，乃由於異寵之錫，豈鷩冕當用之制乎？然人臣命數，止於其九。自五命至於七命，固有
translation_en:
… praised the achievements of Duke Huan of Qi [天 likely a misprint for 大] while deeming Guan Zhong a man of small capacity!

Record of Rites (Liji)
"Regulation: The Three Dukes, with one additional degree of appointment, wear the dragon robe; if there is such an addition, it is by special bestowal, and does not exceed nine degrees of appointment."
Yang Pu
Examiner Liang, Instructor, comments: Essays on the Classic of Rites value being canonical and regulated; this composition achieves that.
Examiner Wu, Director of Studies, comments: Those in the examination hall who wrote on this topic were mostly disorganized and off the mark; this essay is able to convey the principle through its words, and is truly an outstanding piece on the Classic of Rites.

The [regulations?] for theinvestiture garments of the great ministers, though arising from gracious bestowal, have limits that cannot be transgressed. For the Three Dukes have their regular [system?] of investiture garments; yet when special grace adds to them, it still stops at nine degrees of appointment—how could there be any further transgression beyond that [?]?

The chronicler of the "Royal Regulations" (Wangzhi) states: The former kings established offices and had the Three Dukes—namely, the Grand Preceptor, the Grand Mentor, and the Grand Guardian. Discussing the Way and ordering the state, their responsibility is великий indeed; harmonizing and regulating yin and yang, their duty is weighty indeed. Invested to confer nobility, their regulation receives the honor of eight degrees of appointment [膺 misprinted as 曆]; robed to manifest merit, their regulation uses the insignia of the pheasant cap (bimian). When they receive an addition of one degree of appointment, they reach the rank of nine degrees; occupying the position of an Upper Duke (shanggong), they wear the dragon robe and cap (gunmian) with descending dragons; like the descendants of former kings, they wear the dragon robe without ascending dragons. If, as one of the Three Dukes, one receives the addition of the dragon robe and cap, this comes from a bestowal of special grace—how could it be the regular rule for eight degrees of appointment? And if, as one of the Three Dukes, one receives the augmentation of the dragon robe, this is due to a gift of extraordinary favor—how could it be the standard regulation for the use of the pheasant cap? Yet the number of degrees of appointment for a subject stops at nine. From five degrees of appointment up to seven degrees, there is indeed room to…

title: 成化元年山東鄉試錄
text:
可進矣至於九命之分則截然不可有踰焉自七命
至於八命尚有可加矣至於九命之等則斷然不可
有過焉此先王命服之制所以優待大臣而致謹於
名分之際者何其至歟抑觀古者設官之制其爵以
五其命以三自上公九命以及子男之五命自上公
衮冕以及子男之毳冕所衣之服必從其命其命不
差則其服不僭此先王所以正名分而章服采也讀
者宜通考之
閏月則闔門左扉立于其中皮弁以日視朝遂
以食日中而餕奏而食日少牢朔月大牢五
飲上水漿酒醴酏

title: 成化元年山東鄉試錄
text:
聽朔則所居異其常矣視朝而就養又豈不因時而
異其宜哉記玉藻者知其然謂夫天度運行餘分以
積三歲一閏五歲再閏而閏月有焉人君聽月朔之
事就明堂之室闔門左扉而由其右立于其中而無
所偏闔扉必於其左者以左為陽以陽為正則所居
之異其常矣立必於其中者或於太廟或於旁室則以
居為之位矣然所居之禮如此而所養之禮何如是
故人君服皮弁之服視常日之朝不敢慢於所養也
遂用禮朝之服而□□厚於所養也日中之食不
===
則更造乃朝食之□□□心志而助其氣體又必
作夫音樂以侑之□□□□□□衆唯具羊豕之以牢非
儉也宜也月朔□□備牛羊豕之太牢非奢也稱也
五飲之品以水為上非以本始為貴乎醬酒醴酏以
次而列非以清濁為序乎人君聽朔視朝順天時而
居養如此可謂盡其禮矣大抵人君一身居九重之
尊為萬民之表苟非以禮自防則無以正心以正朝
廷而正天下矣故居養無時不在乎禮而下文又曰
動則左史書之言則右史書之其謹於禮至矣哉
punctuated: 聽朔，則所居異其常矣；視朝而就養，又豈不因時而異其宜哉？記《玉藻》者知其然，謂夫天度運行，餘分以積，三歲一閏，五歲再閏，而閏月有焉。人君聽月朔之事，就明堂之室，闔門左扉而由其右，立于其中而無所偏。闔扉必於其左者，以左為陽，以陽為正，則所居之異其常矣；立必於其中者，或於太廟，或於旁室，則以居為之位矣。然所居之禮如此，而所養之禮何如？是故人君服皮弁之服，視常日之朝，不敢慢於所養也；遂用禮朝之服而□□，厚於所養也。日中之食，不□則更造，乃朝食之□□□心志而助其氣體，又必作夫音樂以侑之。□□□□□□衆，唯具羊豕之以牢，非儉也，宜也；月朔□□，備牛羊豕之太牢，非奢也，稱也。五飲之品，以水為上，非以本始為貴乎？醬、酒、醴、酏，以次而列，非以清濁為序乎？人君聽朔視朝，順天時而居養如此，可謂盡其禮矣。大抵人君一身，居九重之尊，為萬民之表，苟非以禮自防，則無以正心，以正朝廷而正天下矣。故居養無時不在乎禮，而下文又曰：「動則左史書之，言則右史書之。」其謹於禮至矣哉！
translation_en: …proclaim the first day of the month, then the place where he resides differs from his usual practice; when he holds daily court and proceeds to take his nourishment, how could he not also vary what is appropriate in accordance with the season? The compiler of the "Jade-Bead Pendants" (Yuzao) chapter in the Record of Rites knew this to be so. He observed that as the heavenly degrees revolve in their courses, the remaining fractions accumulate so that in three years there is one intercalary month, and in five years two intercalary months; thus intercalary months come to be. When the ruler attends to the affairs of the first day of the month, he repairs to the chambers of the Hall of Light (Mingtang), closes the left leaf of the double door while passing through the right, and stands in the middle of the doorway without leaning to either side. That the closing of the door leaf must be on the left is because the left is yang, and yang represents the regular; thus the place where he resides differs from his usual practice. That he must stand in the middle of the doorway—between the Grand Ancestral Temple on one side and the adjacent chamber on the other—means he takes his temporary abode as his ritual position. Now, since the rites for his residence are like this, what of the rites for his nourishment? Therefore, the ruler wears the white deer-skin cap (pibian) to hold daily court, not daring to be negligent toward that which nourishes him; and he immediately dines still wearing the ceremonial court attire […], showing how generously he treats his nourishment. For the midday meal, he does not [prepare new dishes?], but rather consumes the leftovers of the morning meal. [In order to養? nourish his] mind and will and to sustain his vital energy and physical body, he also must have music performed to encourage his appetite. [On ordinary days when affairs are?] numerous, only the lesser sacrifice (shaolao) [?] of sheep and swine is provided—this is not out of frugality, but because it is fitting. On the first day of the month […], the grand sacrifice (tailao) of ox, sheep, and swine is prepared in full—this is not out of extravagance, but because it matches the occasion. Among the five kinds of drink, water is placed at the top: is this not because what is fundamental and original is esteemed? Fermented grain beverage [?漿], wine, sweet new wine, and thin rice gruel are arranged in sequence: is this not ordered according to their clarity and turbidity? When the ruler proclaims the first day of the month and holds daily court, adapting his residence and nourishment in accordance with the heavenly seasons in this manner, he may truly be said to have fulfilled the rites to the utmost. In general, the ruler in his own person occupies the exalted position of the ninefold palace and serves as the exemplar for the myriad people. If he does not restrain himself by means of ritual propriety, he will have no way to rectify his mind so as to rectify the court and rectify all under Heaven. Thus in his residence and nourishment there is no moment that does not rest upon ritual propriety. Moreover, the text below goes on to say: "When he acts, the Scribe of the Left records it; when he speaks, the Scribe of the Right records it." How supreme indeed is his attentiveness to ritual propriety!

□天下□□□□莫大焉，而謂「德主天下之善」，何也？蓋□德□□□必稱，善乃德之實行。德主於善，則德之見於行者無不實；善無不主，則德之萃於已者無不成。德而不主於善焉，則無以得一本萬殊之理，而德非其德矣。此德所以必主於天下之善也與！

夫所謂德者，原於天而具於人也。仁、義、禮、智，其德之大端與！然仁不徒仁，必散於事而為仁之善，則自親親而仁民、而愛物，皆是也；義不徒義，必散於事而為義之善，則自從兄而敬長、而尊賢，皆是也；以至君主之敬、夫婦之別，而凡齊莊中正者，何莫非禮之善

title: 成化元年山東鄉試錄
text:
乎是非之明賢否之擇而凡文理密察者何莫非智
之善乎然四德不主於善則無以得一本萬殊之理
仁焉或流於姑息義焉或至於無耻與夫禮與夫智
亦未必不爲苟簡之行術數之陋也是豈所謂德哉
所貴乎德者亦惟以善是主焉仁主仁之善則凡親
親仁民愛物之類皆吾所當擇而自無姑息之弊仁
之德不全於我乎義主義之善則凡從兄敬長尊賢
之事皆吾所當爲而自然無耻之患義之德不備於
我乎禮之德何所□□乎齊莊中正而苟簡之行不
===
形於身體也智之□□所主□乎文理密察而術數
之陋不萌於心思也博而取之不使一善之或遺精
以擇之罔俾一行之或乖善隨所主而愈多德由所
主而益大將見原於天而具於人者有以復於我矣
主善之功其可少耶至哉張子之言發于正蒙實所
以明伊尹告太甲之旨彼謂德無常師主善爲師卽
此德主天下之善與彼謂善無常主協于克一卽下
文所謂善原天下之一與德不主善無以得一本萬
殊之理善不原一無以達萬殊一本之妙傳而承之
punctuated: 乎？是非之明、賢否之擇，而凡文理密察者，何莫非智之善乎？然四德不主於善，則無以得一本萬殊之理。仁焉或流於姑息，義焉或至於無耻，與夫禮、與夫智，亦未必不爲苟簡之行、術數之陋也。是豈所謂德哉？所貴乎德者，亦惟以善是主焉。仁主仁之善，則凡親親、仁民、愛物之類，皆吾所當擇，而自無姑息之弊，仁之德不全於我乎？義主義之善，則凡從兄、敬長、尊賢之事，皆吾所當爲，而自然無耻之患，義之德不備於我乎？禮之德何所□□乎齊莊中正，而苟簡之行不形於身體也；智之□□所主□乎文理密察，而術數之陋不萌於心思也。博而取之，不使一善之或遺；精以擇之，罔俾一行之或乖。善隨所主而愈多，德由所主而益大，將見原於天而具於人者，有以復於我矣。主善之功，其可少耶？至哉，張子之言！發于《正蒙》，實所以明伊尹告太甲之旨。彼謂「德無常師，主善爲師」，卽此「德主天下之善」與？彼謂「善無常主，協于克一」，卽下文所謂「善原天下之一」與？德不主善，無以得一本萬殊之理；善不原一，無以達萬殊一本之妙。傳而承之
translation_en:
… goodness of propriety? The discernment of right and wrong, the selection between the worthy and the unworthy, and everything that involves orderly pattern and close examination—what among these is not the goodness of wisdom? Yet if the four virtues do not take goodness as their master, there is no way to grasp the principle of one root and myriad manifestations. Benevolence might degenerate into lax indulgence, righteousness might lead to shamelessness [?], and as for propriety and wisdom, they too would not necessarily avoid becoming perfunctory conduct or vulgar calculation and artifice. How could this be what is called virtue?

What is valued in virtue is simply taking goodness as its master. When benevolence takes the goodness of benevolence as its master, then all things such as affection for kin, benevolence toward the people, and love for creatures are what we ought to choose; thus there is naturally no flaw of lax indulgence—is not the virtue of benevolence then complete within me? When righteousness takes the goodness of righteousness as its master, then all matters such as obeying elder brothers, respecting elders, and honoring the worthy are what we ought to do; thus there is naturally no trouble of shamelessness [?]—is not the virtue of righteousness then fully realized within me? As for the virtue of propriety, upon what does it [rely for its mastery? It takes as its master] grave reverence and balanced rectitude, so that perfunctory conduct does not manifest in one's person. As for the [virtue] of wisdom, what it takes as its master [lies in] orderly pattern and close examination, so that the vulgarity of calculation and artifice does not sprout in one's thoughts. By gathering broadly, one allows not a single good to be overlooked; by selecting with precision, one lets not a single action go astray. As goodness increases according to what one takes as master, and virtue grows ever greater through what one takes as master, one will see that what originates in Heaven and is endowed in man is restored within oneself. How could the merit of taking goodness as master be slighted?

Supreme indeed are the words of Master Zhang (Zhang Zai 張載)! Set forth in the Correcting Youthful Ignorance (Zhengmeng 正蒙), they truly serve to clarify the purport of Yi Yin's 伊尹 admonition to Tai Jia 太甲. When the latter said, "Virtue has no constant teacher; taking goodness as master is its teacher," is this not precisely "virtue taking the goodness of all under Heaven as its master"? When he said, "Goodness has no constant master; it harmonizes in being able to attain the One," is this not precisely what the text below calls "goodness originating in the One of all under Heaven"? If virtue does not take goodness as master, there is no way to grasp the principle of one root and myriad manifestations; if goodness does not originate in the One, there is no way to reach the subtlety of myriad manifestations returning to one root. Seeking it broadly [?] …
